feedback: If gaps are left, highlight the uncovered stretch: 'this bit wasn't measured — the clips don't cover all of the book yet'

If the first clip starts inset from the edge or the last stretch is left uncovered, prompt: 'start right at one end and keep going to the other end — the length is the number of clips that SPAN the book'; if the leftover bit is shorter than one clip, agree it is 'about' or 'a bit more than' that many clips
When the span is fully tiled flush with no gaps or overlaps, confirm the count is now an honest length: the number of clips that cover the book end to end
For the home-made ruler, point out that each mark is just where one unit ends and the next begins
activities.intendedInsight: A length is the number of equal units that completely fill an object from end to end; gaps, overlaps, or a row that starts inset mean the count does not yet report the true length.
learnerActions: Lay identical paper clips along a book, starting flush at one end, so they continue end to end to the far end with no gaps and no overlaps
Run a finger along the book from the very start to the very end to check that the clips cover ALL of it

Report the length as the number of clips that span the book; if the last clip sticks out past the end or a small bit is left that is shorter than a clip, say 'about' or 'a bit more than' that many clips
Repair a row that someone else laid with obvious gaps or overlaps, nudging the clips flush until the whole span is tiled
Build a small ruler by snapping copies of a single clip into a row, to see that a ruler is just units lined up
activities.title: Measure a book with paper clips, filling the whole span

feedback: If the child accepts a gappy row's count, point to the gap: 'is every bit of the pencil covered? the clips skip this part, so the count isn't the whole length'
Praise diagnosing the specific error ('there's a gap here', 'these overlap', 'it starts too late') over simply restating a number
After repair, have the child re-run the finger-sweep to confirm full coverage
activities.intendedInsight: A count is only a length when the units completely tile the span; spotting and fixing gaps/overlaps is the child's job, not something to accept on trust.
learnerActions: Look at a row laid by a 'mixed-up' puppet that has visible gaps, overlapping units, or units that start in the middle
Explain what the puppet did wrong
Re-lay the units correctly so they fill the span flush, end to end, with no gaps or overlaps, and give the corrected length
Judge a stated count (e.g. 'I measured this pencil and got 6') against a row that has an obvious gap, and say whether the number is right
activities.title: Fix the mixed-up puppet's measurement

feedback: If the child says the object with more (smaller) units is longer, lay the two measurements side by side so the equal spans are visible: the object didn't change, only the size of the unit did
If the child mixes big and small clips, ask them to lay one measurement in equal units and compare: 'which count can we trust, and why?'
Confirm the key idea when stated: counts can only be compared when the units are the same size
activities.intendedInsight: More units does NOT mean longer when the units are different sizes; the same object gives a bigger count with smaller units without getting any longer, and mixing unit sizes within one measurement makes the count fail to report a length because each unit covers a different amount.
learnerActions: Measure one object with large clips, then measure the SAME object again with small clips, and compare the two counts
Measure a second object with a jumbled mix of big and small clips, then lay equal-size clips beside it
Answer: 'I measured this ribbon with big clips and got 4, and with little clips I got 8 — did the ribbon get longer? Why did the numbers change?'
Answer: 'Could I measure this with a mix of big and little clips? Why not?'
Optionally run the matches version: compare a row of a few long matches with a row of many short matches that cover the same distance
activities.title: Does 'more units' mean 'longer'? The mixed-size challenge

feedback: If the child counts the points where clips meet (or the clip ends), ask 'what are you counting — the clips, or the joins between them?' and have them touch each clip once
Treat this as a counting slip to tighten, not a conceptual gap — the child who makes it still understands coverage and equal units
Link forward: on a ruler, the number 1 is written at the end of the first unit; it tells us one whole unit has been covered from the 0 end, so we count the spaces covered, not the tick marks
activities.intendedInsight: The length is the number of units (the spaces covered), not the number of marks or junctions where units meet; counting the joins gives an off-by-one answer.
learnerActions: After laying clips along an object, state the count and then point to each thing being counted
Count the units (the clips/spaces), touching each one once, rather than the points where units meet or the end marks
Check a row where the count might be off by one: 'you counted 7 — point to each thing you counted'
activities.title: Count the units, not the joins

feedback: For a chosen gappy or overlapping row, prompt the child to explain whether the whole object is covered
For a mixed-unit distractor, ask whether the units are all the same size and why that matters

If the child says the row with more short units is longer, align the two rows end to end to show the spans match — the object is the same length; only the unit size differs, so the bigger count does not tell us which is longer
When the valid row is chosen, have the child state the two reasons it is valid: equal units AND full end-to-end coverage
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising a valid measurement means checking for full coverage, no gaps/overlaps, and equal units; and when two rows cover the same span, a bigger count made of smaller units does not mean the object is longer.
learnerActions: From several rows laid along an object, choose the one that measures it correctly, where distractors have gaps, overlaps, or mixed-size units
Count the units spanning an object and give the number
Compare two rows that cover the SAME span — a few long units versus many short units — and judge whether the row with more (shorter) units is actually longer, explaining your reasoning
activities.title: Pick the correct measurement (recognition check)
